terminal_record.description_medium: Supplied material describes one Council for National Policy compilation as listing 1,011 names from 1981–2020 while covering fewer than half of its members, and a separate 2020 directory said to contain 426 names. terminal_record.description_long: Supplied material describes two Council for National Policy membership compilations. It says a TrumpFile compilation spans 1981 to 2020 and lists 1,011 names; its compiler reportedly cautions that it covers fewer than half of the council’s members. A separate directory, described as leaked in September 2020, is said to list 426 people. These figures refer to different documents and should not be added or treated as a total membership count. The frozen entry’s January 20, 1981 date does not establish when either list was created or released. The supplied materials do not confirm Donald Trump’s membership, attendance, participation, or a policy action connected to CNP. This draft therefore describes only the supplied list-scope claims and does not assert a Trump-related event. The counts and dates remain unverified, and a dated membership or participation source, or an explicit scope decision to treat this as CNP history, is needed to resolve the hold.

terminal_record.description_long: According to the supplied entry, Deutsche Bank maintained a lending relationship with Donald Trump beginning in the late 1990s and extending into the 2000s. The account says the bank’s private-wealth division financed Trump National Doral and hotels in Chicago and Las Vegas despite earlier casino bankruptcies and defaults. It gives an aggregate above $640 million, but the supplied research note warns that the figure may combine a Chicago construction loan with later private-wealth loans rather than represent one verified portfolio total. The record also says congressional Democrats subpoenaed bank records during Trump's presidency and that the information was not made public; no specific subpoena or release history is established in this draft. It alleges the lending created financial leverage that foreign intelligence services could exploit, a concern rather than a demonstrated consequence. The packet does not settle loan amounts, dates, divisions, or project allocations. All these details remain allegations or uncertain figures from the supplied record; no motive or wrongdoing is established. This internal draft is not publication-eligible.

terminal_record.title: CARES Act expanded business-interest deductions for leveraged firms
terminal_record.description_short: The CARES Act temporarily raised the business-interest deduction limit, a change tax advisers said could benefit highly leveraged firms, including private-equity funds.
terminal_record.description_medium: Congress.gov lists the CARES Act as Public Law 116-136, signed March 27, 2020, and says Section 2306 increased the business-interest deduction limit for 2019 and 2020. Congressional Research Service and Holland & Knight explain that the cap rose from 30% to 50%; tax advisers said this could help leveraged businesses and private-equity funds. The sources do not substantiate the packet’s $1.5 billion figure or its claim that lobbyists inserted the provision without scrutiny.
terminal_record.description_long: On March 27, 2020, the CARES Act became Public Law 116-136. Section 2306 temporarily raised the cap on deductible business interest from 30 percent to 50 percent for tax years 2019 and 2020. Congressional Research Service explained that the amendment also let firms use 2019 income when calculating the 2020 cap. Holland & Knight’s April 2020 tax analysis said additional deductions could reduce cash taxes or create or increase net operating losses for highly leveraged businesses, including private-equity funds and their portfolio companies. This supports a narrow description of the law’s tax treatment of borrowing costs and its potential benefit to leveraged firms. The sources do not establish the frozen entry’s $1.5 billion estimate, lobbyist authorship, or claim that the provision was inserted without committee scrutiny. Those allegations are omitted rather than treated as facts. The card describes an enacted, broadly applicable tax rule and does not infer that private equity alone received it or that the change produced a particular realized benefit.
